opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot. Prompting is really powerful. You can get a surprising amount of behavior out of a good base model just by giving it the right instructions, a few examples, maybe a scaffold for tool use. But prompting is limited by what the model already "wants" to do. You're steering it within its existing distribution, and you can't steer it very far.

RL fine-tuning lets you change that distribution. When you train against a reward, whether it's a verifiable signal like "did the code pass the tests" or "did the agent actually complete the task in the environment," the model learns behaviors that are hard to describe in a prompt. Things like knowing when to backtrack, when to call a tool versus reasoning on its own, how to recover from a bad intermediate step, or how long to think before committing to an answer. Those are strategies more than instructions, and you can't really write them down. They have to be discovered through trial and error.

There's also a reliability issue. With prompting you might get an agent that works 60% of the time on a multi-step task, and the failures compound over long horizons. RL pushes on exactly those failure modes because the reward is tied to the end outcome, not to whether each step looks plausible. So you get agents that are more robust across long trajectories.

And for practitioners, I think the exciting part is that this is becoming accessible. You don't need a frontier lab to do it anymore. If you have a well-defined task and a way to score outcomes, you can take a smaller open model, do some RL on your specific environment, and often beat a much larger general model that's just being prompted. That specialization angle, getting a small model to be really good at your particular workflow, is where I see a lot of the practical value.

That said, I don't see it as either-or. Prompting is still how you prototype, explore the task, and figure out what the reward should even be. RL is what you reach for once you know what "good" looks like and you want the model to get there consistently.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that prompting is really about eliciting capabilities that are already latent in the model. You're steering it, you're giving it context, you're showing it examples, but fundamentally you're working with whatever distribution the pretrained model already has. And that gets you surprisingly far, which is why so many people stop there.

But when you're building agents, especially agents that need to reason over multiple steps, call tools, recover from errors, and actually complete a task end to end, you start hitting a wall. The failure modes are things like the model gets 80 percent of the way through a trajectory and then does something silly on step seven, or it never learned to verify its own intermediate results, or it's just not calibrated about when to call a tool versus when to think more. You can patch some of that with better prompts, but every patch is brittle, and you end up with these enormous system prompts that are essentially trying to hand-write a policy.

What RL fine-tuning gives you is the ability to actually optimize for the outcome you care about. Instead of telling the model how to behave, you define what success looks like, whether that's a verifier, a unit test passing, a correct final answer, a user accepting the result, and you let the model discover the behaviors that get it there. And the behaviors it discovers are often things you would not have thought to prompt for. You see models learn to backtrack, to double-check, to decompose problems in ways that are specific to the domain. That's the part that I find really exciting, because it means the model is learning a policy over long horizons rather than just imitating a surface pattern.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this is where the data story changes. With supervised fine-tuning you need demonstrations, and good demonstrations of agentic behavior are expensive and often don't exist. With RL you need environments and reward signals, which is a different problem, and honestly it's a harder engineering problem in a lot of ways, but it scales differently. Once you have a good environment, the model can generate its own experience. So a lot of the work we do is really about building those environments and getting the reward right, because the model will absolutely exploit any gap in your reward, and that's where most of the practical difficulty lives.

So to summarize, prompting is about steering, and RL is about actually teaching the model a new policy for a task. For reasoning agents, where the hard part is the multi-step, error-prone, tool-using behavior, I think that distinction really matters.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prompting with RL fine-tuning generally, but does not mention OpenAI’s advice or its use of RL fine-tuning to build the deep research agent.

r002.rationale: It describes prompting as steering or telling the model how to behave, while RL optimizes outcomes and teaches a policy for multi-step reasoning behaviors such as backtracking and checking work.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is between eliciting a capability and training a capability. With prompting, you’re giving the model instructions or examples that help it use what it already knows. That can take you quite far, including getting it to break a problem down, use tools, or check its work. But the model’s parameters aren’t changing.

With RL fine-tuning, you give the model opportunities to try different approaches, get feedback, and update its behavior based on what succeeds. For a reasoning agent, that can mean learning when to call a tool, how to respond when a tool fails, or when to revise an approach instead of continuing down an unproductive path. You’re training those decisions across a sequence of actions.

The hard part is the feedback. If you have a verifiable outcome, you have a useful signal. If your reward only loosely captures what you want, the agent can learn to satisfy that reward without actually becoming more useful. And even with a good outcome signal, figuring out which decisions contributed to success can be difficult.

So I see prompting and RL as complementary. Prompting helps you establish what the model can do and define the task. RL can make successful behaviors more consistent, provided you have the right environments and feedback. The real test is whether those behaviors carry over to new problems.

r002.rationale: It describes prompting as providing instructions or examples and RL fine-tuning as updating behavior based on feedback across sequences of reasoning-agent decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prompting is a very powerful starting point. You can ask a model to break a problem down, use tools, or check its work, and often get much better results. But you’re still working with the behaviors the model already has. The question with RL is whether we can make the behaviors that lead to successful outcomes more reliable through training.

For an agent, that matters because success depends on a sequence of decisions. What should I do next? Do I have enough information? Should I call a tool, or try a different approach? With RL, you can let the model attempt a task, evaluate the outcome, and use that feedback to improve its policy. You don’t necessarily have to prescribe every intermediate step.

The hard part is the feedback. If you have an outcome you can verify, you have a useful training signal. If your reward only loosely captures what you want, the model can get better at satisfying that reward without becoming a better agent. So I see prompting and RL as complementary: prompting helps you explore what’s possible and define the task, while RL can help turn successful behavior into something more consistent. Whether it actually generalizes is something you have to measure.

r002.rationale: It says RL can improve an agent’s policy from outcome feedback and that prompting helps define the task, but it does not clearly identify RL as reinforcing the model’s reasoning process in contrast to prompting supplying instructions.
